item.title: Trump clears $2.1 bn Patriot missile deal for Ukraine after Zelenskyy tensions: Is his Ukraine policy changing?
item.description: The US has approved a $2.1 billion sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine after weeks of tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Allies will help finance the purchase, but delivery delays remain a concern as Kyiv seeks protection from Russian attacks. What does this mean for US policy on Ukraine?
item.dc:creator: Swati Gandhi
item.content:encoded: After weeks of tension between US President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Washington on Friday (local time) approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles to Kyiv, the State Department announced.According to Reuters, the sale of 500 Patriot missiles has been approved at an estimated cost of $2.1 billion, in what is being considered one of the most significant steps to supply defensive weapons to war-torn Ukraine since the start of the second Trump administration. US approves Patriot missile sale for Ukraine: What we knowThe development comes at a time when Ukraine has long said it urgently requires more missile interceptors to defend against increasingly large Russian missile attacks. The Patriot system is Kyiv's most effective defence against high-speed ballistic missiles.Delayed missile deliveries have added to a growing list of tensions for Ukraine, especially after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia and waived sanctions related to Moscow under the Graham Act. The US President also slammed Zelenskyy for the country's unwillingness to stop attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure.Earlier this week, the Ukrainian President said that Kyiv had been waiting for over a month for Washington to sign off on critical missile supplies as Russia intensified its attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure across the country.According to the report, despite its urgent need, Ukraine is likely to face a lengthy wait for the interceptors. Arms deals often take years to complete, and two people briefed on the US decision said the missiles have yet to be built, with deliveries not expected until the early 2030s.Who's paying for the 500 Patriot missiles?In a statement, the State Department announced that Kyiv will pay for these 500 Patriot missiles with contributions from Canada, Germany, and Norway channelled through a programme called US JUMPSTART, along with national funds financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan.The department said, "This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe."It further noted, "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan."According to a Pentagon website, the US JUMPSTART programme allows allies to make donations to buy weapons, services, and training for Kyiv to support its self-defence following Moscow's invasion.Previously, the JUMPSTART programme was used in August to purchase 3,350 air-launched cruise missiles worth $825 million made by Zone 5 Technologies and CoAspire.What's changing in Trump's Ukraine policy?The Patriot sale suggests that Washington remains willing to supply defensive weapons to Ukraine despite Trump’s recent criticism of Zelenskyy. However, the purchase is being financed through allied contributions and European Union-backed funds. Alongside Trump’s diesel deal with Russia and sanctions waivers, the approval points to continued military support for Kyiv without establishing a broader change in Washington’s approach to the war.(with agency inputs)

item.title: France's credit outlook splits rating agencies: Fitch turns negative, Moody’s stays stable, bond risk sees biggest drop
item.description: Fitch warned that France’s debt outlook is worsening, projecting debt to reach 124% of GDP by 2028 amid weak growth. Moody’s kept its Aa3 rating unchanged. Despite a recent rally that narrowed the French-German bond spread, fiscal concerns and budget challenges persist.
item.dc:creator: Bobins Vayalil Abraham
item.content:encoded: Credit ratings agency Fitch on Friday revised France's outlook to "negative" from "stable", warning that deteriorating fiscal conditions and political fragmentation are undermining debt stabilization prospects.The agency pointed to weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider deficit since its August review, compounded by a fractured political landscape that is making sustained fiscal consolidation harder to deliver.Why Fitch downgraded France's outlookFitch predicted that the debt level for the European Union's second biggest economy would rise from nearly 115.7 percent of GDP in 2025 to 124 percent in 2028. In its last review in August, Fitch had forecast that France's debt would reach 122.7 percent of GDP in 2028. "Weaker growth, renewed fiscal deterioration and higher yields have increased the challenge of delivering the necessary sustained fiscal consolidation to arrest France's worsening debt trajectory," Fitch said.According to Fitch’s outlook, the prospects for debt reduction after the presidential election in April-May next year were "uncertain".It said the political divisions, with far-right and far-left candidates leading opinion poll surveys, would make it difficult to agree "a credible fiscal strategy"."The emerging policy debate ahead of the presidential election has not materially strengthened Fitch's confidence in the prospects for durable deficit reduction that could lead to debt stabilization. Large protests over public services and living costs further complicate the social context for fiscal consolidation," it said. International investors have expressed widespread concern over France's debt level and this has pushed up the interest yields it pays to service debt, which is one of the highest in Europe. The outlook revision adds to pressure on the government ahead of more planned protests this weekend, underscoring the political challenges of implementing spending cuts and deficit-reduction measures. French bond risk falls French 10-year yields hit their highest since 2002 last week at more than 5.14%, rising more sharply than those of most peers, reflecting greater sensitivity to shifts in market confidence amid concerns over France's fiscal trajectory, struggle to pass a budget and social unrest. Earlier, the INSEE national statistics agency reported Friday that the economy has not grown so far this year and contracted in the period from July to September. Meanwhile, France on Friday managed to avoid another rating downgrade, this time by Moody’s. Moody’s kept France’s rating steady at Aa3 with a negative outlook. The following markets rally has led to French bond risk being poised for its biggest drop since the 2020 pandemic. According to Bloomberg, the extra yield investors demand to hold 10-year French bonds, known as OATs, over safer German debt fell 13 basis points to 154 basis points on Monday, the largest drop in six years on a closing basis.
